channel.title: TaskIAP journal
channel.description: Sticky notes, journal entries and reports on construction project management.

item.title: Write Down Why Each Date Is What It Is
item.description: The pour is Thursday. Why Thursday? Someone knows: the rebar inspection is booked Wednesday afternoon and the pump truck is free Thursday. The schedule only shows a bar starting Thursday.

item.title: Panama Canal: Logistics and Health Came First
item.description: France started the Panama Canal in 1881 and quit after years of work. Thousands of workers died of yellow fever and malaria, and the sea-level design didn't suit the ground.

item.title: How the Panama Canal Got Built
item.description: France spent eight years and thousands of lives and failed. The United States finished it in ten. The difference was mostly planning: health, housing, logistics and a design that fit the ground.

item.title: Why does a quiet site worry me?
item.description: A crew that jokes around is a crew that talks. A cartoon on the trailer whiteboard about the sticking valve keeps more people away from it than last month's report. If nobody jokes, they're probably not passing on what they know either.

item.title: Measure How Long Crews Wait Before Starting
item.description: The shift starts at 7:00. The first tool touches the work at 7:50. In between there's the toolbox talk, a permit that isn't signed yet, a search for the right fittings, and a wait for the hoist.

item.title: What do you do with the person who annoys everyone?
item.description: Most difficult people have one habit that's useful in the right job. The one who checks every bolt callout catches the wrong grade before the pour. Move them to where that habit helps instead of trying to train it out of them.

item.title: Base Percent Complete on Records
item.description: On most status reports, percent complete is a number someone types in. It goes up a few points a week because nobody wants to argue, then sits at 95 for three months.

item.title: Plan Around Spring Load Restrictions
item.description: Every spring, when the frost comes out of the ground, a lot of Ontario roads go on reduced loads. A precast delivery or a crane move that was fine in February might not be allowed on the same road in April.

item.title: Turn Lessons Into Checklist Changes
item.description: Every job ends with a lessons-learned report. It goes in the closeout binder and the next team never opens it. They're busy, it's forty pages, and half the lessons say "communicate better".

item.title: Why do some crews act like they're just passing through?
item.description: Maybe because we treat them that way. A shared desk, a chair, Wi-Fi that works and a locker that locks are cheap. Give them to everyone, including the cleaners, yard hands and apprentices. People notice who got a spot and who didn't.

item.title: Replace Lags With What They Stand For
item.description: A five-day lag between two activities usually means one of three things: concrete curing, waiting on a permit or inspection, or a guess someone made two years ago. The schedule doesn't say which.

item.title: Empire State Building: A Logistics Job
item.description: The Empire State Building went up in about thirteen months in 1930 and 1931. The steel frame rose several floors a week. It finished early and under budget.

item.title: Record the Field Cost of Every Change
item.description: A change order prices the extra work: material, hours, markup. It usually doesn't price what the change does to the work around it. Crews get pulled off their sequence, finished work gets torn out, the same room gets visited three times.

item.title: Why is field data still on paper?
item.description: A crew-hour costs more than a phone, and phones are allowed on almost every site, so it isn't cost or rules. I think it's the apps: most can't be used with gloves on, in the rain, in a few seconds, so foremen write it down and somebody types it in later. Start with the timesheet, because everyone fills that in.

item.title: Follow Every Open Item to a Name and a Date
item.description: Ask why a task isn't done and it takes three phone calls to find out. The crew is waiting on scaffold. Scaffold is waiting on a permit. The permit is waiting on a signature from someone at their cottage with no cell signal.

item.title: Put Winter Heat in the Budget and the Schedule
item.description: A January pour in Ontario needs hoarding, heaters, fuel, blankets and someone checking temperatures overnight. None of that is usually an activity on the schedule, so nobody plans it. It gets sorted out one cold morning at a time.

item.title: Why do hand-drawn roadmaps stick around so long?
item.description: No dates, no logic, no owners, so nobody can prove them wrong. Draw the picture from the schedule instead. Then it changes when the schedule changes, and it can't turn into a second version of the job.

item.title: Hold Lessons Sessions at the End of Each Phase
item.description: The usual lessons-learned meeting happens at closeout, when the superintendent from the foundation work has been on another job for a year and the foreman who solved the tie-in has retired.

item.title: The Quebec Bridge Collapses of 1907 and 1916
item.description: The Quebec Bridge fell twice while it was being built, killing 88 workers. The first collapse is still taught as a case of a warning that didn't reach the site in time.

item.title: Show What Changed in Each Schedule Update
item.description: Every monthly update comes in as a new set of PDFs. To see what changed, someone has to compare it to last month's page by page. Usually nobody does, so changes go unnoticed: a finish date moved a week, a logic tie got deleted, a duration got shorter with no explanation.

item.title: Is a short video the best protection against claims?
item.description: I think so. A lot of claims come down to what an area looked like on a certain day. Thirty seconds of video from that day settles it. Attach the clip to the item it's about, so it's filed before anyone knows they'll need it.

item.title: Sydney Opera House: Construction Started Before the Design Was Done
item.description: The Sydney Opera House was supposed to take four years. It took fourteen, opened in 1973, and cost many times the first estimate.

item.title: Long Stretches of Overtime Cost More Than They Recover
item.description: One Saturday gets you a day. Six weeks of Saturdays doesn't get you six days. People get tired, make more mistakes, get hurt more and start missing Mondays. Hours go up and output per hour goes down.

item.title: Price Risks in Days
item.description: A risk heat map puts each risk in a coloured square. The colour doesn't tell you what the risk does to the finish date, so the meeting argues about whether it's red or orange.

item.title: Who signs when the signer is on vacation?
item.description: Usually nobody, and the job finds out at the first hold point that stalls. Write it down: who can sign for whom, for what, and until when, before the vacation starts.

item.title: Locates Expire
item.description: You call for locates before you dig in Ontario, and the locates are only good for a set time. If the excavation slips past that date, you need them done again, and that takes days the schedule didn't allow for.

item.title: Ask What You'd Do Differently on Day One
item.description: "Improve communication with the design team." "Plan procurement earlier." These show up in every lessons-learned report and change nothing, because nobody can act on them.

item.title: Why does the consultant's report sound familiar?
item.description: Because they spent the first month interviewing your superintendent. Hire consultants for narrow, rare problems, like a forensic metallurgist. For running the work, spend the money on your own people, since they're the ones who live with the result.

item.title: Keep Two Weeks of Ready Work Ahead of Each Crew
item.description: Work is ready when everything it needs is in place: drawings issued, material on site, permit signed, area handed over, the work before it finished. If one thing is missing, it isn't ready, no matter what the schedule shows.

item.title: Hoover Dam: How They Cooled the Concrete
item.description: Concrete gives off heat as it cures. Poured as one solid mass, the Hoover Dam would have taken more than a century to cool, and it would have cracked.

item.title: Walk the Laydown Yard
item.description: Walk the yard before you read the reports. Material that showed up months early is money already spent, sitting in the rain, getting lost or damaged. Empty racks for next week's work mean a crew will be standing around soon.

item.title: How many milestones does a job have?
item.description: On paper, a couple of hundred. Only three or four matter, like the freeze-up window or first energization. Pick those at the start and protect them. If every date is treated as critical, crews stop believing any of them are.

item.title: Treat the Crane as Part of the Schedule Logic
item.description: Two lifts that need the same crane can't happen at the same time. That's as firm as rebar before concrete. Most schedules keep the logic in one place and the resources in another, and nobody checks one against the other.

item.title: Lessons Learned That Change the Next Job
item.description: Most lessons-learned work ends up as a report nobody reads. A few habits turn lessons into changes the next job will use.

item.title: Do small cuts and strains tell you anything?
item.description: Not about fatalities. But they repeat for the same reasons: the same knife, the same task, the same corner of the yard, and the fixes are usually cheap. You'll only see the pattern if reporting one takes less than ten seconds.

item.title: Put Holdback on the Schedule
item.description: Under Ontario's Construction Act, the 10 percent holdback isn't paid when the work feels finished. It follows steps: substantial performance is certified and published, the lien period runs out, then the holdback is paid.

item.title: Build a Mockup of the Hard Details
item.description: A curtain wall corner, a firestopped penetration, a shower pan: details that repeat hundreds of times in a building and are easy to get slightly wrong.

item.title: Group Hold Points by Who Clears Them
item.description: Five hold points need the same inspector this week. They get booked as five separate visits because five foremen each called on their own.

item.title: What is the one form everybody fills in?
item.description: The timesheet, because it gets them paid. Add one question per task: done, partial or blocked, with a photo if it's blocked. It takes a minute at the end of the shift, and the schedule is up to date every night.

item.title: Brooklyn Bridge: Bad Wire and a Safety Margin
item.description: Partway through building the cables of the Brooklyn Bridge, the engineers found out a supplier had been sending wire that failed inspection. The rejected wire had been switched back into the deliveries. A lot of it was already in the cables.

item.title: Count Drawing Revisions
item.description: "Design is 90 percent complete" can stay true for a year. A better measure is how many drawings were revised this month, and how many of those had already been issued for construction.

item.title: Put Site Rules Into the Schedule Checks
item.description: No hot work within 10 metres of fuel. Two people for a confined space entry. Hold for the inspector before backfill. These rules are in a binder, a toolbox talk and the superintendent's head. The schedule doesn't know any of them.

item.title: Is a bad attitude the person or the job?
item.description: Mostly the job. Give someone ready work, the right tools and straight answers and most of it goes away. The few who hide problems, fudge progress or cut safety corners should go quickly, because everyone is watching what you put up with.

item.title: A Night Shift Needs a Supervisor
item.description: A second shift gets added to catch up. The superintendent leaves at six, and the night crew works from a list. Nobody on site can make a decision.

item.title: Apply for Utility Connections Early
item.description: Permanent hydro, gas, water and telecom connections are late on job after job. The utility has its own queue, its own design review and its own crews, and none of that is on your schedule.

item.title: Why do so many schedule activities finish on a Friday?
item.description: My guess: people plan in weeks, not days. The work doesn't care what day it is, so Monday takes the slip.

item.title: Track Expiry Dates on Permits, Tags and Tickets
item.description: Permits, scaffold tags, crane certifications, welding tickets, medicals, insurance certificates, the concrete mix approval. Almost everything that allows work to happen has an end date, and the schedule doesn't know any of them.

item.title: Quebec Bridge: The Warning Came Too Late
item.description: In 1907 the Quebec Bridge collapsed during construction and killed 75 workers. Days before, the inspector on site had reported that steel members were bending.

item.title: Planning From Constraints
item.description: Most schedules are built from activities and logic ties. Most work on site is stopped by something else: a permit, a crane, a missing part, the weather. Here is what changes when you plan from the conditions instead.

item.title: Has anything ever been 50 percent complete?
item.description: Reports show 10, 90 and 95 all the time. 50 hardly ever shows up. Maybe that's the point where people start paying attention.

item.title: Plan for the Learning Curve on Repeated Work
item.description: Repeated work gets faster. The tenth floor, the fortieth pipe support and the hundredth panel all go faster than the first as the crew learns the details, the sequence and each other.

item.title: Closeout Takes Longer Than Planned
item.description: Deficiencies, commissioning, turnover documents and closeout often take a third of the calendar. They get planned as the last 5 percent of the work, and nobody manages them until the crews are leaving.

item.title: How long should a coordination meeting be?
item.description: Long enough to get every red item to a name and a date. If that takes two hours, the meeting isn't the problem.

item.title: Keep a Crane Pick Log
item.description: The crane is usually the busiest piece of equipment on site, and nobody knows how busy it is. The plan assumes a number of picks per hour. The operator knows the actual number.

item.title: Water Test the Envelope Before Finishes
item.description: Water finds the one gap in the window flashing, but usually after the drywall is up, the flooring is down and the owner has been invited for a walkthrough.

item.title: Answer What-If Questions in the Meeting
item.description: "What happens if the crane is two weeks late?" On most jobs the answer is "we'll look at it and get back to you". The answer comes a week later, after the decision has already been made by default.

item.title: What do good superintendents have in common?
item.description: They walk the site before they open the laptop. Small sample, could be a coincidence.

item.title: Transcontinental Railroad: Paid by the Mile
item.description: The two companies building the first transcontinental railroad in the 1860s were paid in government bonds and land for every mile of track they laid. So both went as fast as they could and quality came second.

item.title: Adding Crews to One Area Can Slow It Down
item.description: When a job falls behind, the first move is usually to add crews. Put four trades in one room and they wait for each other, get in each other's way and damage each other's work. Output per person drops, sometimes enough that the room finishes later.

item.title: Use Old As-Built Schedules for Estimating
item.description: At closeout, the actual dates for every activity go into the archive and nobody looks at them again. They're the best estimating data a contractor has: your own crews, your own jobs, your own weather.

item.title: Is a high RFI count bad?
item.description: Not sure. It can mean bad drawings, or a crew that asks instead of guessing. How long the answers take matters more than how many there are.

item.title: Write Down the Estimate's Assumptions
item.description: Every estimate rests on assumptions: the soil matches the geotech report, the steel comes in one shipment, the owner picks finishes by spring. They get decided quickly and nobody writes them down.

item.title: Review Serious Near Misses Like Injuries
item.description: A near miss has everything an injury has except the injury: the same broken process, the same missing barrier, the same rushed decision.

item.title: Has a lessons-learned report ever changed the next job?
item.description: Only when the lesson got written into a checklist the next team had to use.

item.title: Why Closeout Takes a Third of the Job
item.description: Deficiency lists, commissioning and turnover get planned as the last 5 percent of the work and managed when the crews are leaving. Here is why that goes wrong and how to run it from the start.

item.title: Check All Contractors' Plans Against Each Other
item.description: The civil contractor plans to close the north road next week for trenching. The steel contractor plans deliveries on the north road next week. Each schedule looks fine on its own.

item.title: Crossrail: The Systems Were Late, Not the Tunnels
item.description: London's Crossrail, now the Elizabeth line, finished its tunnels on time. The line was supposed to open in December 2018. A few months before, the delay was announced. It opened in May 2022, billions over budget.

item.title: Who owns the float?
item.description: The contract says one thing and everyone acts like it's theirs. In practice, whoever uses it first.

item.title: Make the Lookahead Longer Than Your Longest Lead Time
item.description: A three-week lookahead won't catch something that takes four weeks to clear. Permits, engineered supports, crane bookings, shutdowns: if clearing it takes longer than the lookahead, it's already late when it shows up.

item.title: Make It Easy to Ask Questions
item.description: On every site, asking a question costs something. Part of it is time: finding the person who knows and waiting for an answer. Part of it is looking like you should already know. When asking costs too much, people guess, and some of those guesses get built.

item.title: Small Jobs Train Project Managers Faster
item.description: A three-year project gives a project manager one full cycle to learn from. Three-month jobs give them four cycles a year.

item.title: What counts as a weather day?
item.description: Whatever the contract says, which is rarely what the crew thinks. Agree on it before the first storm.

item.title: Photograph Work Before It's Covered
item.description: Rebar before the pour. Conduit and pipe before the drywall. Underground services before backfill. Once it's covered, people have to guess, and guessing usually means cutting and patching.

item.title: Check the Schedule Against Hard Rules Before Issuing It
item.description: A schedule can put two crews in one confined space, skip a hold point, or plan a lift over a live line, and the software will print it anyway.

item.title: Why does the crane end up running the job?
item.description: Because every trade needs it and only one can use it at a time. If you want the real schedule, look at the crane booking sheet.

item.title: Big Dig: The Wrong Epoxy
item.description: Boston's Big Dig moved an elevated highway into tunnels. It finished in 2007, years late and billions over the early estimates.

item.title: Count the Handoffs
item.description: Schedules count tasks. Most of what goes wrong happens between tasks, when work, information or authority passes from one crew, company or system to the next.

item.title: Staff the First Month After Handover
item.description: The job can finish on time and under budget, and the owner will still remember that the heat didn't work the first week, the keys were wrong and nobody answered the phone.

item.title: Does anyone remember last week's toolbox talk?
item.description: Probably not the words. Maybe the story, if there was one. So tell them about something that happened on this site.

item.title: A Short History of Scheduling, From Gantt to Monte Carlo
item.description: Every tool on a scheduler's screen was invented to fix one particular problem. Knowing which problem tells you where each tool is still weak.

item.title: Put Owner Decisions on the Schedule
item.description: Owner decisions hold up work just like late steel does: finish selections, change approvals, a tie-in date, a design question. They're rarely on the schedule, so they never show as late.

item.title: Why does nobody believe the baseline?
item.description: Because everyone knows it was built to win the job, not to run it. Keep it for the contract and plan from the current forecast.

item.title: Channel Tunnel: Frequent Survey Checks
item.description: In 1990 the British and French tunnelling crews broke through to each other under the Channel. They had started from opposite coasts, many kilometres apart. The two tunnels met within a fraction of a metre.

item.title: Measure How Long Bad News Takes to Reach the Schedule
item.description: Every problem has two dates: the day someone on site first saw it, and the day it showed up in the schedule. On most jobs that gap is days or weeks, and the whole time, decisions are being made from a schedule that's wrong.

item.title: Match the Paperwork to the Risk
item.description: A temporary laydown pad doesn't need the paperwork of a pressure boundary. Four days spent perfecting it are four days taken away from work that affects the finish date.

item.title: Why does the schedule review take two hours?
item.description: Because we go through the whole schedule. The crews only need the next three weeks and the five things holding them up.

item.title: Give a Range With Every Instruction
item.description: Drawings say ±5 mm. Instructions say "ASAP". The crew can't tell a hold point from a favour, so they treat everything as urgent and wear themselves out on work that could have waited.

item.title: Tell the Crew When to Stop
item.description: "Hydrovac the copper lines, 3 days" gets you three days of digging whether you need it or not. "Hydrovac until you can see the layout, a day at most" tells the crew when they're done.

item.title: Check the Logic Before Trusting Float
item.description: One missing logic tie and an activity shows eight days of float it doesn't have. One padded duration and a path looks critical when it isn't.

item.title: Is a mockup ever a waste of money?
item.description: I haven't seen one that was. Whatever goes wrong on the mockup would have gone wrong four hundred times on the building.

item.title: Give Suppliers Real Dates
item.description: Suppliers can tell when your must-have date has two weeks of padding in it. Pad it and they stop telling you about problems in their shop until it's too late to work around them.

item.title: Keep Requirements Where Operations Can Find Them
item.description: The fire code calls for a two-hour wall. That requirement gets copied into the design basis, a wall type, a firestop detail, a QC record and a commissioning check. Then the job closes out and the copies get scattered.

item.title: Why does every Ontario job lose a week in March?
item.description: Mud, frost coming out of the ground, load restrictions on the roads, and everyone sick of winter. Plan for it.

item.title: Schedule Each Recurring Inspection Separately
item.description: Weekly scaffold inspections go into the schedule as one 200-day bar. That bar can't be late, so nobody notices when this week's inspection is.

item.title: Ask Whether a Loss Can Be Undone
item.description: Safety programs focus on what can kill people, not on what happens most often. Project risk can work the same way.

item.title: The Rideau Canal
item.description: In six years, with hand tools, a British army engineer and a few thousand labourers built a navigable route from Ottawa to Kingston. It cost several times its estimate, it cost hundreds of lives, and it is still in use.

item.title: What is the cheapest schedule fix there is?
item.description: Calling the inspector the day before. Second is having the material on site before the crew shows up.

item.title: Keep Good Crews Together
item.description: The plan prices six welders at a rate. A crew that has worked together all season will outperform six welders who met on Monday, at the same rate.

item.title: Use Weather Records and Forecasts in the Schedule
item.description: Weather is the one project risk with a free daily forecast that comes with probabilities. Most schedules still plan a February pour the same as a June one.

item.title: Should foremen see the whole schedule?
item.description: Probably not. Three weeks of their own work and what's holding it up. The rest doesn't help them.

item.title: Count New Problems and Count the Checks
item.description: You can't list what you don't know you don't know. You can count how many new problems turn up each week.

item.title: Scan Material at Every Handoff
item.description: A pipe spool gets fabricated, shipped, received, staged and installed, and each step is recorded in a different system. Finding one still takes three phone calls and a walk through the laydown yard.

item.title: Make Signing Off Quick
item.description: A hold-point sign-off can mean a drive across site, a binder and a pen. So people save them up and do a batch, or sign without looking.

item.title: Does a good-looking Gantt chart mean a good plan?
item.description: No. A messy one updated this morning is worth more than a tidy one from last month.

item.title: Write Procedures as Steps
item.description: A procedure in a PDF is a document people may or may not follow. What the crew does is a series of steps, checks, hold points and qualifications.

item.title: Clear the Constraint That Frees the Most Work
item.description: Status meetings ask what happened yesterday. The more useful question is which blocked item, if cleared today, would free up the most work.

item.title: The Critical Path Changes
item.description: Run a schedule a thousand times with realistic weather and delivery ranges and the critical path often changes from run to run. The one on the printout is just one of them.

item.title: Why does winter cost more than the heat?
item.description: Bulky gear, short days, frozen equipment, and Monday mornings spent thawing things out. The fuel bill is just the part you can see.

item.title: Recheck Assumptions on a Schedule
item.description: Ground conditions, vendor capacity, "the permit will be renewed": written down at the start of the job and never looked at again. An assumption is a risk nobody has checked yet.

item.title: Keep Every Forecast, and Rebaseline When Needed
item.description: Two winters and forty change orders later, the job is still being measured against the plan from day one, and the difference is called variance.

item.title: How the CN Tower Was Built
item.description: The CN Tower was built in about three and a half years in the 1970s. The concrete shaft went up on a form that moved continuously, and a helicopter set the antenna on top. Most of the lessons are about choosing the method and keeping the supplies coming.

item.title: Who should run the lessons-learned session?
item.description: Someone who wasn't on the job. People will tell an outsider things they won't say in front of their boss.

item.title: Keep the Whiteboard and the Schedule in Sync
item.description: The schedule has five thousand activities. The site runs off a whiteboard that covers three weeks and gets updated at 6 a.m. You need both: the contract needs the full schedule, and the crews need this week.

item.title: Everything That Stops Work Is a Constraint
item.description: A predecessor, a missing spool, an unsigned permit, a crane booked somewhere else, wind over the lift limit, a room too crowded to work in, a radiation dose budget nearly used up. On most jobs those are tracked in seven different places. They're all the same kind of thing: something that has to be true before work can start.

item.title: How many crane picks fit in an hour?
item.description: Fewer than the plan says. Rigging, signals and wind take up more of the hour than the lifts do.

item.title: Watch for Closing Windows
item.description: A pour needs three dry days. The crane leaves in October. In-water work has to stop when the fish spawning season starts. None of those are logic ties, and most schedules don't include them.

item.title: Name the People the Job Depends On
item.description: The schedule says two Class B welders. The job needs Dave, the only one qualified on that alloy, and Dave is at his daughter's wedding until Tuesday.

item.title: Record Field Information Once
item.description: Foremen write down what happened every day. Then the same information gets typed again into the schedule update, the timesheet, an RFI, a QC record and, years later, a claim.

item.title: What should a new PM do on day one?
item.description: Walk the site with the superintendent and listen. Read the schedule on day two.

item.title: Use One Breakdown Structure
item.description: The estimate, the schedule, the cost report and the work packages each have their own breakdown structure. They match at the start of the job. By month six there are four versions and a weekly meeting to reconcile them.

item.title: Put a Name on Every Green Status
item.description: Anyone can mark a status green, so reports drift optimistic. Often green just means nobody wanted to argue.

item.title: Is it okay to have fun on a job site?
item.description: It should be. Crews that joke around talk more, and people who enjoy the work stick around. If you need a break from schedules, there's a small idle game here about growing a lemonade stand into a galactic empire.

item.title: Track How Sure the Finish Date Is
item.description: SPI and CPI measure work done against the plan. Nothing measures how well we know the finish date, and that's what the owner cares about. A job can report green every month while the finish keeps slipping.
